en: Majjhima Nikāya 142:
The Discourse on the Analysis of Offerings.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, taking a pair of new cloths, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī...
He said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this pair of new cloths was personally woven by me for the Blessed One, spun by my own hand.
May the Blessed One accept it from me out of compassion.”
When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
“Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī.
When it is given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.”
A second time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this new pair of robes was personally woven by me, specifically for the Blessed One.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept it from me out of compassion.”
A second time, the Blessed One said this to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
“Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī.
When it has been given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.”
A third time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this new pair of cloths was spun by my own hand and woven by my own hand for the sake of the Blessed One.
May the Blessed One accept it from me out of compassion.”
A third time, the Blessed One said this to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
“Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī.
When it is given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.”
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One accept, venerable sir, the new pair of garments from Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
She has been very helpful to the Blessed One, venerable sir—she is his maternal aunt, his nurse, his foster-mother, and the one who gave him milk.”
He gave the Blessed One breast milk when his mother had passed away.
The Blessed One, venerable sir, was also of great benefit to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
It was by coming to the Blessed One, venerable sir, that Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī went for refuge to the Buddha, went for refuge to the Dhamma, and went for refuge to the Saṅgha.

Venerable sir, it is by relying on the Blessed One that Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has abstained from taking life, abstained from taking what is not given, abstained from sexual misconduct, abstained from false speech, and abstained from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence. Venerable sir,
it is by relying on the Blessed One that Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has come to possess verified confidence in the Buddha,
verified confidence in the Dhamma, and verified confidence in the Saṅgha, and she is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones.

“Venerable sir, it is by relying on the Blessed One that Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has become free from doubt regarding suffering, free from doubt regarding the origin of suffering, free from doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and free from doubt regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
The Blessed One, venerable sir, has been of great benefit to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
“It is so, Ānanda; it is just so.”
Ānanda, when one person, having relied upon another, has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—
I say that it is not easy for this person to repay that person by means of prostrating,
rising up, joining the palms in salutation, performing respectful duties, or by providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Ānanda, when one person, by relying on another person, abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—
I say, Ānanda, that it is impossible for this person to repay that person adequately; that is to say:
by saluting, rising up, joining the palms in reverential salutation, performing acts of respect, and by providing robes, almsfood, lodgings,
and medicinal requisites for the sick. For, Ānanda, when one person, by relying on another, comes to possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha, in the Dhamma, and in the Saṅgha,
and possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones— Ānanda, it is through this that this person [is benefited] by that person.
I do not say that it is easy to repay by means of salutations,
rising to greet, joining the palms in reverence, performing acts of respect, or by providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
For, Ānanda, when one person, depending on another, becomes free from doubt regarding suffering and free from doubt regarding the origin of suffering...
He is free from doubt regarding suffering, he is free from doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and he is free from doubt regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Ānanda,
I say that it is not easy for this person to repay that person by means of prostrating,
rising to greet, joining the palms in salutation, performing respectful services, or by providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Moreover, Ānanda, there are these fourteen kinds of personal offerings.
What are the fourteen?
One gives a gift to a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
This is the first gift to an individual.
One gives a gift to a paccekabuddha—
this is the second gift to an individual.
One gives a gift to a disciple of the Tathāgata who is an arahant—
this is the third personal offering.
One gives a gift to one who has entered upon the way to the realization of the fruit of arahantship—
This is the fourth kind of personal offering.
One gives a gift to a non-returner—
this is the fifth kind of personal offering.
One gives a gift to one who has entered upon the way to the realization of the fruit of non-returning—
this is the sixth personal offering.
One gives a gift to a once-returner...
This is the seventh gift to an individual.
One gives a gift to one who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of once-returning—
this is the eighth gift to an individual.
One gives a gift to one who has entered the stream—
this is the ninth personal offering.
One gives a gift to one who has entered upon the way to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry—
This is the tenth kind of personal offering.
One gives a gift to an outsider who is free from lust for sensual pleasures—
this is the eleventh kind of personal offering.
One gives a gift to a virtuous worldling—
this is the twelfth personal offering.
One gives a gift to an immoral worldling—
This is the thirteenth gift to an individual.
One gives a gift to an animal—
this is the fourteenth gift to an individual.
In this regard, Ānanda, having given a gift to one who has gone to the animal realm, a hundredfold merit is to be expected;
having given a gift to an immoral worldling, a thousandfold merit is to be expected; having given a gift to a virtuous worldling, a hundred-thousandfold merit is to be expected;
and having given a gift to an outsider who is free from passion for sensual pleasures, a hundred-thousand-millionfold merit is to be expected.

An offering may be expected [to yield fruit]; when one has given a gift to someone practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, an incalculable and immeasurable offering may be expected;
what need is there to speak of one who is a stream-enterer? What need is there to speak of one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning?
What need is there to speak of a once-returner? What need is there to speak of one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning?
What need is there to speak of the non-returner? What need is there to speak of one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship?
What need is there to speak of an arahant? What need is there to speak of a paccekabuddha? What need is there to speak of a Tathāgata, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha?
Moreover, Ānanda, there are these seven kinds of offerings made to the Saṅgha.
What are the seven?
One gives a gift to both Sanghas with the Buddha at their head—
this is the first gift dedicated to the Sangha.
When the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, one gives a gift to both Saṅghas—
this is the second kind of offering directed toward the Saṅgha.
One gives a gift to the community of bhikkhus.
This is the third kind of offering made to the Saṅgha.
One gives a gift to the community of bhikkhunīs—
this is the fourth kind of offering made to the Saṅgha.
‘Please designate so many bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs from the Saṅgha for me’—
this is the fifth gift dedicated to the Saṅgha.
‘Please designate so many bhikkhus from the Saṅgha for me’— he gives a gift [in this way].
This is the sixth gift pertaining to the Saṅgha.
‘Appoint so many bhikkhunīs for me from the Saṅgha,’ he gives a gift—
this is the seventh gift pertaining to the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in the future there will be those of the lineage who wear the saffron robes around their necks, yet are immoral and of evil character.
People will give gifts dedicated to the Saṅgha for the sake of those immoral ones.
Even then, Ānanda, I declare that a gift given to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable.
But I do not say, Ānanda, that by any means a gift given to an individual is more fruitful than a gift given to the Saṅgha.
There are, Ānanda, these four purifications of gifts. What four?
“Ānanda, there is an offering that is purified by the giver, not by the recipient.
Ānanda, there is an offering that is purified by the recipient, not by the giver.
Ānanda, there is an offering that is purified neither by the giver nor by the recipient.”
“Ānanda, there are offerings that are purified both by the giver and by the recipient.
And how, Ānanda, is an offering purified by the giver but not by the recipient?
Here, Ānanda, the giver is virtuous and of good character, while the recipients are immoral and of evil character.”
In this way, Ānanda, a gift is purified by the giver, not by the recipient.
And how, Ānanda, is a gift purified by the recipient, not by the giver?
Here, Ānanda, the giver is immoral and of evil character, while the recipients are virtuous and of good character.
In this way, Ānanda, a gift is purified by the recipient, not by the donor.
And how, Ānanda, is a gift purified neither by the donor nor by the recipient?
Here, Ānanda, the donor is immoral and of evil character, and the recipients are also immoral and of evil character.
In this way, Ānanda, a gift is purified neither by the giver nor by the recipient.
And how, Ānanda, is a gift purified both by the giver and by the recipient?
Here, Ānanda, the giver is virtuous and of good character, and the recipients are also virtuous and of good character.
“In this way, Ānanda, an offering is purified both by the giver and by the recipient.
These, Ānanda, are the four purifications of offerings.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“He who, being virtuous, gives a gift to those who are immoral,
having acquired it righteously and with a mind full of serene confidence;”
Having full faith in the sublime fruit of action,
that gift is purified by the donor.
When one who is immoral gives a gift to those who are virtuous, [that gift is purified].
That gift which is obtained through unrighteousness by one with a lack of faith,
who does not believe in the sublime fruit of karma—
that offering is purified only by the recipient.
When one who is immoral gives a gift to those who are immoral,
having acquired it by unrighteous means with a mind lacking faith,
not believing in the sublime fruit of kamma—
I do not say that such a gift yields abundant fruit.
But when one who is virtuous gives a gift to those who are virtuous,
having acquired it righteously and with a mind full of serene confidence—
Having full confidence in the sublime fruit of action,
that gift indeed I call one of abundant fruit—
when one who is free from passion gives a gift to those who are free from passion.
Having acquired it in accordance with the Dhamma,
with a mind full of serene confidence and placing deep faith in the sublime fruit of kamma—
this indeed is the foremost of all material gifts.
The Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅgasutta, the twelfth, is finished.
The Vibhaṅga Chapter, the fourth, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Bhaddekaratta, Kaccāna, Lomasakaṅgiya, Asubha; Mahākamma, Saḷāyatana, and Vibhaṅga.
The summary recitation is the Truth of the Elements;
[this is] the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta.
